data.title: 74 out of every 100 consumer loan applications were for phones this Diwali
data.description:
India's festive shopping season is increasingly being financed by credit, with consumer-durable loan applications rising 22% during Diwali 2026 compared with last year, even as demand shifts towards smaller towns and rural markets.
 
Data from lending technology platform Lentra for November 1-9, 2026, show that rural India accounted for 58% of consumer-durable loan applications, compared with 42% from urban India. Tier-3 towns also edged past metropolitan cities, pointing to a widening geographical base for consumption financed through borrowing.
 
The numbers suggest that festive credit demand is no longer concentrated in large cities. Smaller towns and rural markets are emerging as important drivers of purchases ranging from smartphones and televisions to refrigerators and washing machines.
 
 
The average consumer-durable loan ticket size stood at an estimated Rs 28,000, indicating the scale of purchases being financed through credit. 
Diwali 2026: What India's Credit-Fuelled Purchases Looked Like Across States
 
 Young Indians lead festive borrowing
 
The age profile of borrowers highlights the growing importance of younger consumers in the festive credit market. Around 62% of consumer-durable loan applicants were below 35, with the 22-35 age group emerging as the typical borrower segment.
 
Mobile phones dominated the borrowing basket. Nearly 74 out of every 100 consumer-durable loan applications were for mobile phones, while the remaining 26 were spread across other categories of consumer durables.
 
The concentration of demand in smartphones points to their continued importance as a primary consumption purchase among younger borrowers. Men aged 22-25 were particularly prominent in mobile-phone financing, according to Lentra's analysis.
 
However, the pattern changes when gender and age are considered together. Women showed a stronger preference for financing household appliances, particularly in the 35-plus age group.
 
Women's borrowing patterns reveal a different consumption story
 
Women accounted for 31% of consumer-durable loan buyers in urban areas, compared with 24% in rural markets.
 
The difference suggests that women's participation in credit-financed consumption remains higher in cities, although their share of borrowing in rural markets is also significant.
 
The data also point towards a different product preference among women. While men typically borrowed for mobile phones, appliance purchases were more prominent among women aged 35 and above.
 
Women's two-wheeler borrowing provides another insight into changing consumption aspirations. Of every 100 women's two-wheeler loan applications across city tiers, 57 were for motorcycles, 39 for scooters and mopeds, and four for electric two-wheelers.
 
 India's festive shopping basket changes from state to state
 
The state-level numbers reveal how consumption preferences vary significantly across markets.
 
Gujarat and Rajasthan were particularly smartphone-driven markets. Mobile phones accounted for 86% of consumer-durable loan applications in Gujarat, compared with the national average of 74%. In Rajasthan, the share stood at 82%.
 
Television financing was more prominent in southern India. LED TVs accounted for 13.6% of consumer-durable loan applications in Telangana and 12.4% in Tamil Nadu, against a national average of 7.4%.
 
Refrigerators featured more prominently in eastern and southern markets. They accounted for 6.8% of applications in West Bengal and 6.6% in Karnataka, compared with the national average of 4.6%. Madhya Pradesh also recorded a higher share at 6.1%.
 
In northern India, washing machines emerged as a stronger category. They accounted for 15% of consumer-durable loan applications in Punjab, against the national average of 4%. Haryana recorded an 8.3% share, while Delhi stood at 6%.
 
The data also reveal distinct demand patterns in other states. Air conditioners accounted for 6% of applications in Andhra Pradesh, 2.5 times the national share of 2.4%. Maharashtra stood out for audio systems, which accounted for 2.1% of applications compared with the national average of 1.6%.
 
In Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, inverters and batteries had a higher share of applications at 1.3% and 1.1%, respectively, compared with the national average of 0.6%.
 
Key highlights: 
 
  • Mobile phones lead festive consumer-durable financing with a 74% national share
  • Gujarat and Rajasthan lead in mobile phone financing, with the category accounting for 86% and 82% of applications, respectively.
  • Southern states show a stronger preference for LED TVs, while refrigerators and washing machines feature more prominently across several other markets.
  • Consumer-durable loan applications grew 22% over the previous festive period, with rural markets accounting for 58% of applications.
  • In Telangana and Tamil Nadu, LED televisions accounted for a notably higher proportion of applications than rest of the states. 
  • Telangana recorded a 13.6% share, followed by Tamil Nadu at 12.4%.
  • Refrigerators featured more prominently across West Bengal, Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh, accounting for 6.8%, 6.6% and 6.1% of applications, respectively.
  • In Punjab, washing machines accounted for 15% of consumer-durable loan applications. Haryana recorded an 8.3% share, while Delhi stood at 6%.
  • In Andhra Pradesh, air conditioners accounted for 6% of applications, 2.4%. Maharashtra recorded a relatively higher share of audio system financing at 2.1%
  • In Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, inverters and batteries accounted for 1.3% and 1.1% of applications
 
" India does not have one festive shopping basket. What is significant is where this demand is coming from. With rural markets contributing 58% of applications and Tier-3 towns edging past metros, festive credit activity is clearly extending beyond the largest cities," said Rajesh Kumar, CEO, Lentra.

data.title: Explained: Sarvam AI's Token Factory and debate over AI sovereignty goals
data.description:
Indian artificial intelligence startup Sarvam AI has announced Token Factory, offering access to multiple models, including its own and those developed in China, through a unified inference platform. The announcement has sparked debate over India's homegrown AI ambitions. The matter has come under scrutiny because Sarvam is among the companies selected under the government's IndiaAI Mission to develop homegrown AI models.

What is Sarvam AI’s Token Factory

Sarvam AI’s Token Factory is a platform that allows businesses and developers to use different artificial intelligence (AI) models through a single service, without having to set up or manage their own computing infrastructure. According to the company, it runs Sarvam’s own AI models as well as other open-weight models, including DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi and Google’s Gemma, on GPU clusters located in India. Users can access these models through a single application programming interface (API), which allows their applications to connect to the AI service and send requests.
 
 
The platform handles the process of running an AI model and generating responses to users’ questions or instructions. This process is called inference. Sarvam says its system is designed to make this process faster and more cost-effective by managing how requests are sent to its GPUs and reusing parts of earlier prompts where possible. Businesses can choose a model depending on their requirements and pay based on the number of tokens processed. Tokens are small units of text that an AI model reads or generates.

How Sarvam’s Token Factory functions

Sarvam describes Token Factory as an inference stack serving its own and other open-weight models from GPU clusters in India. Its catalogue includes Sarvam 105B, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and V4 Pro, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM 5.3 and Flash, and Gemma 4 31B. Developers access them through one OpenAI-compatible API by configuring the endpoint, selecting a model and sending requests.
 
The platform manages the work between a request and a response through three layers:
  • An inference engine
  • A cache
  • A control plane
The engine runs the model on graphics processing units (GPUs). The cache stores reusable prompt information to avoid processing the same context repeatedly. The control plane manages requests, routes them to the appropriate resources and adjusts capacity according to demand.
 
The engine separates processing into prefill and decode. Prefill reads the full prompt, including earlier conversation or context. Decode generates the answer one token at a time. Sarvam says these tasks run on separate GPU pools because they have different computing requirements. This can prevent long prompts from slowing response generation for other users.
 
Caching is useful in long conversations and AI agent workflows, where a model may receive the same context repeatedly. Without it, the system processes those tokens again, adding cost and delay. Sarvam says its multi-tier cache uses GPU memory and shared storage to reuse prompt information. A cache-aware router can direct returning requests to servers where relevant context is available.
 
Sarvam charges for input, cached input and output tokens, with rates varying by model and listed in rupees per million tokens. It says it serves more than 450 billion tokens a day through DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. The aim is to provide access to several models without requiring customers to maintain the underlying infrastructure. 
ALSO READ: AI is giving hackers a head start. What's at risk for essential services?

Why has Token Factory triggered a sovereignty debate

The central criticism is that a model’s country of origin differs from the country where it is hosted. DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM were developed by Chinese companies. Running their open-weight versions on Indian GPUs does not make them Indian, transfer their intellectual property to Sarvam or give India control over their development. This raises the question of whether India is building its own AI capabilities or mainly providing infrastructure to run models developed elsewhere.
 
The term covers the ability to set rules for how AI systems are developed and used, audit their behaviour, protect sensitive information and maintain access to critical computing resources. It is therefore broader than data localisation or the nationality of a model developer.
 
Sarvam’s role in India’s AI ecosystem has intensified the debate. It was selected under the IndiaAI Mission, which seeks to strengthen domestic AI capabilities, including indigenous foundation models, and received subsidised computing resources to train its own models. This has raised questions about whether government support for developing homegrown AI was also benefiting a commercial platform offering access to Chinese AI models.
 
Sarvam said its Token Factory does not use government-subsidised GPUs. Co-founder Pratyush Kumar told Moneycontrol that the platform runs on privately procured GPUs. The company said its subsidised access under the IndiaAI Mission, used to train its own models, ended in March 2026. It maintains that developing its own models remains its core mission, while offering other models generates revenue.
 
According to the report, Sarvam argues that model development is expensive and inference can generate revenue from computing infrastructure. It says Indian businesses should be able to use global models through a domestic provider, with local infrastructure and rupee pricing. Global cloud providers such as Amazon Web Services also offer businesses access to AI models developed by other companies through platforms such as Amazon Bedrock.
 
Data sovereignty is another concern. Sarvam says Token Factory runs AI models on its GPU infrastructure in India and does not send customer prompts to the overseas providers that developed those models. The company also says it offers zero data retention on request, under which prompts and responses are not stored. However, keeping data in India does not automatically address every security concern.
 
Businesses also need to examine how data is accessed, how long it is retained and what security measures are in place. Hosting a foreign-developed model in India also does not make the model indigenous.

What about other Indian AI platforms

Sarvam AI has faced greater criticism not only because it is hosting Chinese AI models. Other Indian companies, including E2E Networks and IndieRouter, also offer access to foreign-developed models through infrastructure located in India. E2E Networks, for instance, launched its Blaze inference platform on November 2, 2026, offering models such as DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM and Gemma through a single API. However, Sarvam's position is different because it was selected under the government's IndiaAI Mission to develop indigenous foundation models and has been seen as an important part of India's effort to build its own AI technology.
 
The criticism has therefore centred on whether a company backed by the government to develop homegrown AI should also build a commercial business around models developed in other countries, particularly China. The Indian Express reported that the reaction was partly driven by the expectations attached to Sarvam as a symbol of India's AI ambitions. Supporters, however, argue that hosting foreign models can be a business opportunity and allow Indian companies to serve customers using locally available computing infrastructure.

 

ALSO READ: AI is giving hackers a head start. What's at risk for essential services?
 How does hosting foreign models benefit Sarvam
Chinese AI companies have developed several powerful open-weight models, including DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM. Unlike some AI services that can only be accessed through a company's own platform, open-weight models can be downloaded and run on a company's own servers. This makes them an option for businesses that want to use advanced AI models without relying on services such as OpenAI or Anthropic.
 
For Sarvam, offering these models gives it another source of business besides developing its own AI models. It can attract companies that want to use models such as DeepSeek or Kimi but do not have the GPUs or technical resources to run them themselves. Sarvam provides the computing infrastructure and access through its Token Factory platform.

data.title: IndusInd Bank shares jump 8% on volume surge, near 52-week high
data.description:
Shares of IndusInd Bank rose over 8 per cent on Friday after the company's counter saw a strong volume surge amid traction in banking stocks. Today's rally also pushed the stock close to its 52-week high of 1,077.85.
 
The bank’s counter at 03:07 PM was trading 8.2 per cent higher at ₹999.90 per share on NSE. In comparison, Nifty 50 was up 1.10 per cent at 25,360.85. In intraday trade, the stock rose 8.4 per cent to touch the day's high at ₹1,001 per share.
 
IndusInd Bank recorded a traded volume of 182.05 lakh shares, with a total traded value of ₹1,786.52 crore. The bank's total market capitalisation stood at ₹77,856.04 crore, while its free-float market capitalisation was ₹65,709.17 crore.
 
 
Notably, the Nifty Bank index hit a new high of 64,636, gaining nearly 2.5 per cent on the National Stock Exchange in Friday’s intraday deals, surging over 3 per cent in the past two trading days. 
 
IndusInd Bank Q2 show 
IndusInd Bank posted a sequential improvement in business momentum, profitability and asset quality, even as net interest margins moderated during the second quarter of FY27. The bank reported a 9 per cent quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) increase in average total loans, while average deposits grew 7 per cent. Its loan book stood at ₹3.63 trillion at the end of September 2026, up 11 per cent year-on-year, while deposits rose 10 per cent to ₹4.29 trillion.
 
The bank said asset quality continued to improve, with moderation in stressed loan pools and lower slippages. Gross non-performing assets (GNPA) declined to 2.73 per cent in Q2 FY27 from 3.25 per cent in the previous quarter, while net NPAs fell to 0.83 per cent from 0.95 per cent. Fresh NPA additions also declined to ₹1,460 crore from ₹1,660 crore in Q1 FY27. The bank's provision coverage ratio stood at 70 per cent, while its restructured book reduced to 0.04 per cent of net advances.
 
Vipin Kumar, AVP research at Globe Capital Market, said that IndusInd Bank is moving in a higher highs and higher lows formation within an upward-sloping channel formation since May 2025. Today, it witnessed a bullish break from a 10-day congestion range and also crossed above the gap zone left during its fall on September 24, 2026. “Going ahead, we expect it to test the ₹1,050–₹1,100 levels in the near term, which also represents the upper band of the channel formation,” he said. 
 
Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited. They do not reflect the views of Business Standard. Readers are advised to exercise discretion.

data.title: PV Krishna Reddy raises ₹6,700 cr to buy uncle's stake in Megha Engineering
data.description:
By Dipika Lalwani
 
Indian billionaire PV Krishna Reddy has secured about ₹6,700 crore ($720 million) from global private credit investors to buy out his uncle’s stake in Megha Engineering & Infrastructures Ltd., according to people familiar with the matter, in a layered transaction that is one of the country’s biggest deals this year. 
The consortium of lenders involved in the financing include Davidson Kempner Capital Management, Varde Partners and Elham Credit Partners, the people said asking not to be identified discussing private details.
 
Reddy set up a special purpose vehicle, Provantage Infra Pvt., for the transaction which offered two tranches of three-year secured bonds worth ₹1,750 crore each at a base rate of return of 17.75 per cent and an equity-linked upside payment, the people said. Proceeds are earmarked for acquiring shares in Megha, with the debt secured partly by a pledge over 19.99 per cent of the infrastructure firm, they said. The notes have an option to be extended by up to 12 months, the people added. 
Provantage separately offered as much as ₹2,700 crore of 18-month bonds carrying a 16 per cent coupon and a fourth tranche of ₹500 crore of notes with a tenor of less than three years, according to the people. 
 
 
A representative for Elham Credit Partners declined to comment. Megha Engineering, Davidson Kempner and Varde Partners didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. 
 
The financing highlights the growing role of private credit in India in funding large, complex transactions that can be difficult to execute through traditional bank financing. The transaction would be among the largest new-money private credit deals this year in the country. Shapoorji Pallonji Group’s $1.6 billion fundraising in July was largely used to refinance existing debt.
 
Krishna Reddy, the managing director of Megha Engineering who owns 57 per cent of the company, raised the money to help finance his acquisition of the remaining 43 per cent stake held by his uncle Pamireddy Pitchi Reddy, the executive chairman, Bloomberg News reported in August.
 
Pitchi Reddy did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
 
Founded in 1989 as a small fabrication unit in Hyderabad, Megha Engineering has projects in more than 20 countries spanning tunnels, ports, highways, water systems and power assets, according to its website.
 
India’s private credit sector has doubled in size over the past five years to about $25 billion in assets under management at the end of 2025, according to Moody’s Ratings. That pales in comparison with the US market which manages more than $1 trillion in assets.

data.title: Andhra govt to explore SMR nuclear plants as alternative to thermal power
data.description:
The Andhra Pradesh government on Friday approved tapping nuclear power employing Small Modular Reactor (SMR) technology, advanced nuclear reactors, as an alternative to thermal power, an official said.

K Vijayanand, special chief secretary (Energy), said the southern state would explore setting up nuclear power plants using SMR technology at "retiring thermal power units or other suitable locations in the state after SMR technology is stabilised." "Government, after careful consideration of the request of the Managing Director, APGENCO (Andhra Pradesh Power Generation Corporation), hereby accord approval to explore establishment of a Nuclear Power Plant using SMR technology, as an alternative to thermal power," Vijayanand said in a Government Order (GO).

 

The special chief secretary noted that the private sector will be allowed to participate in Andhra Pradesh's endeavour to set up SMR nuclear power plants.

data.title: Shivraj Singh Chouhan unveils India's 1st home-grown H5N1 bird flu vaccine
data.description:
Union minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan unveiled the country's first indigenously developed H5N1 vaccine to protect chickens from bird flu here on Friday.

The vaccine has been developed by the ICAR-National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases in Bhopal, officials from the Union Agriculture Ministry said.

This is the first-of-its-kind vaccine developed in India against the H5N1 virus of Clade 2.3.2.1a of the highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), they said.

Speaking on the occasion, Chouhan said, "This vaccine is an example of India's self-reliance." HPAI, commonly known as bird flu, is a serious disease affecting chickens and other birds. Outbreaks can result in almost 100 per cent mortality among infected birds.

 

Besides the Union Agriculture Minister, Madhya Pradesh Sports and Youth Welfare and Cooperatives Minister Vishwas Sarang and Bhopal BJP MP Alok Sharma, among others, were also present at the ceremony held here.

data.title: IBPS PO Mains Result 2026 today: Check steps to download PDF scorecard
data.description:
The Institute of Banking Personnel Selection (IBPS) will release the Probationary Officer (PO) Mains Result 2026 today, November 20. The IBPS PO Main exam result will be available late evening, according to information on the official website.
 
Candidates who appeared for the Common Recruitment Process for Probationary Officers/Management Trainees (CRP PO/MT-XVI) can check their results on the official website, ibps.in.

How to check IBPS PO Mains Result 2026?

Step 1: Visit the official IBPS website at ibps.in.
 
Step 2: On the homepage, press on the "CRP PO/MT" link.
 
Step 3: Click on the link that says "IBPS PO Mains Result 2026."
 
Step 4: Fill in your registration/roll number and password or date of birth.
 
 
Step 5: Enter the captcha code and click on "Login."
 
Step 6: Your IBPS PO result 2026 will display on the screen.
 
Step 7: Check your section-wise and total marks, then download the scorecard.
 
Step 8: Take a printout and keep it safe for the next phase.

Details mentioned on IBPS PO Mains Result 2026

After accessing the results, individuals should carefully examine the data shown on the results page. Candidates must check their personal details and follow the official process if they notice any error. 
 
The specifics included may vary based on the format of the document issued by IBPS, and they could consist of:
 
Candidate's name
 
Roll number and registration number
 
Examination name
 
Qualifying status
 
Marks or score details, where provided
 
Instructions regarding the subsequent recruitment stage. 

What after the IBPS PO Mains Result 2026?

Individuals who successfully pass the Mains exams will be invited to participate in the interview phase. The interview timetable and call letters will be published independently on the official IBPS website. 
 
Candidates are advised to commence their preparations by reviewing banking knowledge, current events, and their personal profile information. The ultimate selection will be based on the combined scores attained in both the Mains exam and the interview.

data.title: India's Q3 phone market shrinks 23%, marks decade's weakest festive quarter
data.description:
India's smartphone market recorded its steepest quarterly contraction in several years in Q3 CY2026, with shipments falling around 20-23 per cent year-on-year as rising memory costs pushed device prices higher and weakened demand in the mass-market segment. The decline was accompanied by a shift towards more expensive smartphones, with premium segments holding up better than entry-level and budget devices. Indian smartphone brands also increased their share of the market during the quarter.
 
Data from market research firms CyberMedia Research (CMR) and Counterpoint Research put the market's contraction at 20 per cent year-on-year, while International Data Corporation (IDC) reported a sharper 23.3 per cent decline. IDC estimated smartphone shipments at 36.8 million units during the July-September quarter, marking the steepest quarterly decline since Q4 CY2022. It also described Q3 CY2026 as the weakest festive quarter in a decade.
 
 
Counterpoint, meanwhile, reported that the share of Indian smartphone brands rose from 2 per cent in Q3 CY2025 to 7 per cent in Q3 CY2026.

Entry-level and budget segments take the biggest hit

The divergence between price segments was a key feature of the quarter. According to CMR, shipments in the affordable segment, comprising smartphones priced below ₹7,000, fell 94 per cent year-on-year. The value-for-money segment, covering devices priced between ₹7,000 and ₹24,999, declined 42 per cent. In comparison, the premium segment (₹25,000-₹49,000) grew 38 per cent, while the super-premium segment (₹50,000-₹1 lakh) expanded 32 per cent.
ALSO READ: Apple camera software chief Jon McCormack exits after eight years
Counterpoint reported a 47 per cent decline in shipments of smartphones priced below ₹20,000. It attributed the fall to higher device prices, which pushed several models into higher price bands and made upgrades difficult for price-sensitive consumers.

Memory costs push up smartphone prices

The rise in memory prices has emerged as a major factor behind the market contraction. Higher prices of DRAM and NAND components, driven by demand from AI infrastructure and data centres, have increased the cost of manufacturing smartphones. With limited room to absorb these increases, manufacturers have passed on part of the additional costs to consumers.
 
The impact is visible in average selling prices (ASPs). IDC reported that India's smartphone ASP increased 26.1 per cent year-on-year to a record $371 in Q3 CY2026. Despite the increase in ASPs, the overall market value declined 3.3 per cent, as the fall in shipment volumes outweighed the gains from higher prices.
 
Shubham Singh, research analyst at Counterpoint Research, said, “Q3 marked a realignment for India’s smartphone market, as a memory-led cost squeeze compounded softer consumer demand. Rising component costs pushed device prices higher, putting increasing pressure on affordability and weakening the traditional mass-market volume engine, particularly below ₹15,000.”
 
Rising smartphone prices have also resulted in extended replacement cycles, with consumers reportedly deferring purchases owing to higher device costs and limited upgrades in features and specifications.
 
“Consumers became more selective, extended their replacement cycles and deferred upgrades, while OEMs prioritized margin protection, portfolio rationalization and leaner channel inventory over aggressive volume expansion ahead of Diwali. Sub-₹20,000 shipments declined by 47 per cent in Q3 CY2026 as rising model prices pushed devices into higher price bands,” Singh said.

Festive smartphone sales fall 22 per cent despite financing offers

The pressure on consumer demand continued during the festive season. Counterpoint's preliminary post-festive assessment found that smartphone sales between October 8 and November 10 declined 22 per cent year-on-year, compared with its pre-festive forecast of a 12 per cent decline. Average selling prices increased 28 per cent, keeping market value broadly flat despite lower volumes.
 
Festive discounts also narrowed to 10-25 per cent, compared with 35-40 per cent in 2025, as manufacturers had less room to offer price cuts. Instead, brands relied on no-cost equated monthly instalments (EMIs), bank offers and exchange deals. Counterpoint estimated that 48 per cent of smartphone sales during the festive period were finance-led.
ALSO READ: Explained: Sarvam AI's Token Factory and debate over AI sovereignty goals
Singh said, “This festive season proved that discounts can’t do the heavy lifting when device prices keep climbing. Buyers who needed a phone still bought one, often on EMI, but many others simply held on to what they had. Brands with depth across price bands weathered it well, while those leaning on the entry-level segment took the full force of the price hikes. Overall, smartphone sales this festive season were driven more by need than by festive sentiment.”

Samsung regains top position as Chinese brands lose ground

The market contraction also reshaped the competitive rankings. Samsung reclaimed the top position in Q3 CY2026, followed by Vivo and OPPO, according to CMR and Counterpoint.
 
CMR reported Samsung's market share at 17 per cent, followed by Vivo at 16 per cent and OPPO at 12 per cent. Xiaomi, including POCO, also accounted for 12 per cent, while Apple held a 9 per cent share.
 
IDC's estimates placed Samsung's share at 17.7 per cent, followed by Vivo at 16.8 per cent, OPPO at 13.3 per cent, Apple at 10.1 per cent and Motorola at 8.8 per cent.
 
Samsung was the only brand among IDC's top 10 to record shipment growth, with volumes rising 7.9 per cent year-on-year. IDC attributed its performance to more controlled price increases during the first half of 2026, along with its broad portfolio and scale. Counterpoint, meanwhile, identified the Galaxy A series as the main volume driver for Samsung, supported by its presence across online and offline retail channels.
 
Chinese smartphone brands faced sharper shipment declines during the quarter. IDC attributed this to their dependence on entry-level and budget segments, where rising component costs left manufacturers with less room to absorb price increases. Its data showed Vivo's shipments declining 29.9 per cent year-on-year, OPPO's 26.5 per cent, Xiaomi's 31.1 per cent, Realme's 39.8 per cent and iQOO's 56.5 per cent.
 
CMR's data also showed a 28 per cent decline in Xiaomi's shipments and a 25 per cent decline each for Vivo and OPPO. However, OPPO recorded growth of 45 per cent in the premium segment and 112 per cent in the super-premium segment, even as its value-for-money portfolio contracted 60 per cent.
 
Apple's shipments also declined, with IDC reporting a 25 per cent year-on-year fall. However, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max series accounted for more than 30 per cent of Apple's shipments during the quarter, despite higher launch prices and the absence of a base iPhone 18 model.
 
There were some exceptions among smaller manufacturers. Counterpoint identified Ai+ as the fastest-growing smartphone brand in Q3, with shipments rising 306 per cent year-on-year. Lava recorded 91 per cent growth, while the share of Indian smartphone brands increased from 2 per cent in Q3 CY2025 to 7 per cent in Q3 CY2026, according to Counterpoint.
 
OnePlus was another exception among established brands. CMR reported 27 per cent growth in its overall shipments, with shipments in the sub-₹20,000 segment rising 500 per cent, albeit from a relatively low base.

Premiumisation

The shift towards higher-priced devices is also reflected in IDC's price-band data. Shipments in the $400-$600 segment grew 79.8 per cent year-on-year, while the $200-$400 segment remained almost flat. Together, these price bands accounted for 42.9 per cent of shipments, compared with 29.9 per cent a year earlier.
 
At the other end, shipments of smartphones priced below $100 fell 90.9 per cent to 0.7 million units. Their share of the market dropped from 16.2 per cent to 1.9 per cent.
 
The shift also raises questions about how manufacturers will differentiate their products as the market moves towards higher price points. A separate global study by Techarc, tracking 25 flagship smartphone innovations introduced between 2020 and 2026, found that Samsung led its Brand Innovation Index, while Apple introduced the highest number of innovations. The study found that software and AI features spread across brands faster than hardware innovations.
 
Faisal Kawoosa, chief analyst and co-founder of Techarc, said, “The window in which a first sets a brand apart is shrinking. AI and software features are copied across the industry within months, so they are a weak basis for lasting differentiation. Hardware firsts last longer, but only a few become standard.”

Smartphone market outlook for 2026 and beyond

The market is expected to remain under pressure as elevated component costs continue to affect device affordability and replacement demand. Counterpoint expects the Indian smartphone market to contract around 13 per cent in 2026, while CMR projects an 11-12 per cent decline.
 
IDC expects shipments to fall by more than 25 per cent in Q4 2026, with full-year volumes settling at 125-127 million units, 16-18 per cent below 2025. It expects growth to remain constrained through 2027, with a recovery unlikely before 2028.
 
Tarun Pathak, research director at Counterpoint Research, said, “Entering 2027, the market is likely to remain on a challenging footing, as higher device prices continue to extend replacement cycles and limit volume recovery. Growth opportunities will increasingly shift toward the premium and upper-mid segments, while the mass market remains under pressure from affordability constraints and tighter OEM margins.”

data.title: FD interest rate vs maturity date: What should investors prioritise?
data.description:
If you are a firm believer in traditional investment options such as fixed deposits (FDs), what is the first thing you look at before booking one? For most depositors, it is the interest rate.
 
But there is another factor that often gets overlooked: the FD maturity date.
 
It determines when your money comes back, how long it earns interest and what happens if your financial plans change. Choosing the wrong maturity date could leave you short of funds when you need them, even if you have secured an attractive interest rate.
 
"FD interest compounds over the chosen tenure, so a longer FD usually builds a larger absolute interest amount simply by running longer," Adhil Shetty, chief executive officer of BankBazaar, told Business Standard.
 
 
However, a longer tenure does not automatically translate into a better deal. Banks often offer their most attractive rates on specific tenures, commonly in the one-to-three-year range, rather than on the longest deposits available.
 
Shetty pointed out that a five-year FD at a bank could carry a lower interest rate than its two-year deposit.
 
"It is therefore important to compare interest rates across different tenure options. The best tenure depends on the returns required, money needed in the short term and future financial commitments," said Siddharth Maurya, managing director of Vibhavangal Anukulkara Pvt Ltd.
 

What is an FD maturity date?

 
A fixed deposit offers a fixed interest rate for a specified period. The maturity date is the day the deposit tenure ends, when the bank repays the principal along with the interest earned during the investment period.
 
The maturity date is determined by the date of booking and the tenure selected. Three important aspects of your investment depend on it:
 
Liquidity: The deposit becomes payable on maturity, allowing you to access your money without incurring a premature withdrawal penalty.
Interest rate: The rate agreed upon at the time of booking remains applicable throughout the deposit tenure, irrespective of subsequent market movements.
Reinvestment: What you do with the money on maturity determines how much interest you earn on your next investment.
 
How should you choose an FD maturity date?
 
Matching the FD maturity date with the time when you expect to need the money is a good starting point, according to Shetty.
 
A mismatch could force you to withdraw the deposit prematurely and incur a penalty. Alternatively, your money could remain invested for longer than necessary when you need it for an upcoming expense.
 
"Known short-term expenses or goals usually suit shorter maturities, while funds not needed for several years can be placed in longer ones for a potentially better rate. Keeping a portion in shorter tenures also helps retain liquidity for unplanned needs, rather than locking the entire corpus into one single maturity date," he said.
 
Consider someone who has ₹10 lakh to invest and plans to make a down payment on a house in two years. Would it make more sense to put the entire amount into a single two-year FD or split it across deposits with different maturity dates?
 
Here's how the two options compare.
 
A single two-year FD at an illustrative interest rate of 7 per cent would grow ₹10 lakh to approximately ₹11.49 lakh, making the money available just when the down payment is due.
 
Alternatively, the investor could split the amount between one-year and two-year deposits. This would mean giving up some potential interest on the portion invested for a shorter period, but part of the money would become available after one year.
 
"A single two-year FD, at an illustrative 7 per cent, would grow ₹10 lakh to roughly ₹11.45 lakh exactly when the down payment is due, making it the stronger option if that two-year date is firm. Splitting the amount, say across a one-year and a two-year deposit, sacrifices a modest amount of that return, but makes part of the money available after just one year," Shetty explained.
 
The split-deposit strategy could make more sense if the house purchase timeline is uncertain or the investor may need access to some of the money earlier. 
ALSO READ: Lock in now or wait for higher rates? Here's how to plan your FD strategy
 

Should you choose a higher interest rate or greater flexibility?

 
Consider another situation. A bank offers an investor two options for a ₹10 lakh deposit: 6.5 per cent for one year or 7 per cent for five years. Which one should the investor choose?
 
Locking the entire amount into the five-year FD at 7 per cent would result in a maturity value of approximately ₹14.15 lakh, assuming quarterly compounding.
 
The one-year FD at 6.5 per cent, on the other hand, would grow to approximately ₹10.67 lakh after the first year. The investor would then have to reinvest the proceeds at the prevailing interest rate. If rates rise, subsequent investments could offer better returns. If they fall, the investor could earn less than 7 per cent.
 
"The five-year route offers more certainty, while the one-year route carries potential upside if rates rise, alongside the risk of a lower return if they fall," Shetty explained.
 
In other words, the longer deposit offers certainty over the interest rate, while the shorter one provides greater flexibility but exposes the investor to reinvestment risk.
 
How does FD tenure change your maturity amount?
 
Tenure affects your FD returns in two ways: the interest rate offered by the bank and the number of times interest compounds during the investment period.
 
To understand the difference, consider an investment of ₹10 lakh at a hypothetical interest rate of 7 per cent per annum, compounded quarterly. The following figures are illustrative and do not represent the rates offered by any particular bank.
 
One year
Maturity value: ₹10,71,859
Interest earned: ₹71,859
 
Two years
Maturity value: ₹11,48,876
Interest earned: ₹1,48,876
 
Three years
Maturity value: ₹12,31,439
Interest earned: ₹2,31,439
 
Five years
Maturity value: ₹14,14,779
Interest earned: ₹4,14,779
 
A five-year FD earns approximately 5.8 times the interest generated by a one-year FD in this example, rather than five times. This is because interest also earns interest through compounding.
 
However, the larger maturity amount comes at the cost of keeping your money invested for a longer period.
 

What happens if you withdraw an FD early or renew it automatically?

 
The maturity date also matters when you need to access your money before the deposit period ends or decide what to do with the proceeds.
 
Premature withdrawal can reduce the expected return because banks may levy a penalty or recalculate interest at the rate applicable to the actual period for which the money remained invested.
 
"Premature withdrawal usually triggers a penalty, often around 0.5 per cent to 1 per cent lower than the rate applicable for the period actually held, reducing the final payout below what was expected," Shetty said.
 
The precise penalty and interest calculation vary across banks and deposit products, so investors should check the terms before booking.
 
Automatic renewal is another aspect to watch. If an FD is set up for automatic renewal, the bank generally renews it for the specified tenure at the interest rate prevailing on the maturity date. This rate could be higher or lower than the original one.
 
Reinvestment at maturity also exposes the depositor to the prevailing interest rate cycle.
 
A deposit that was booked when rates were high could mature when banks are offering lower rates, reducing the returns on the next investment. Conversely, a depositor could benefit if rates have risen. 
 

Should you split your FD investment across different tenures?

 
Investors do not necessarily have to put their entire savings into a single deposit. Splitting the amount across different maturities, commonly known as an FD ladder, can help balance returns and liquidity.
 
"You may wish to match the maturity time of your fixed deposits to your financial needs. If you have a financial goal for your child's schooling, holiday or big purchase in less than one year, then a fixed deposit maturing at that point in the future may be appropriate. For longer-term goals, you can look at longer-term deposits. By creating a ladder of short and longer-term fixed deposits, you can allow regular cash flows. This reduces the risk of early withdrawal penalties," said Maurya.
 
For instance, instead of investing ₹10 lakh in a single five-year FD, a depositor could divide the amount into deposits maturing after one, two, three and five years. This allows some money to become available at regular intervals, while the remaining amount continues to earn interest.
 
The right maturity date, therefore, depends not just on the interest rate but also on when you expect to use the money, your need for liquidity and the possibility of reinvesting at a different rate.

data.title: Premium smartphone prices may rise over 30% by year-end: Counterpoint
data.description:
Prices of premium flagship smartphones are expected to go up by 30 per cent to over ₹1 lakh apiece across most of the brands by end of the year due to a sharp rise in memory chip cost, market research firm Counterpoint said on Friday.

Along with the increase in prices of the devices, consumer expectations are also rising, and consumers are looking for meaningful specifications that can match the desired experience across processing speed of the mobile phones, camera, battery, durability, after-sales service, etc.

"A few years ago, a ₹1-lakh smartphone was a rarity in India. Today, as flagship prices keep rising, this price point is becoming increasingly common. Prices of premium flagship devices are expected to rise by more than 30 per cent by the end of 2026 compared with 2025," Counterpoint Research said in a report.

 

Memory prices are expected to account for 43 per cent of the total phone cost by year-end compared to 13 per cent in the first quarter of 2025, as per the report.

"Rising DRAM (temporary storage) and NAND costs, driven by AI data centre demand, have pushed memory's share of smartphone BOM (bill of materials) from about 13 per cent in early 2025 to over 40 per cent, prompting smartphone manufacturers to reassess specifications, components and product strategies to manage costs," said Tarun Pathak, Research Director, Counterpoint Research.

According to the report, Oppo flagship devices have seen the highest jump in the range of 82-87 per cent on a year-over-year (YoY) basis.

Ultra-premium segment market leader iPhone prices have gone up by 20-22 per cent YoY.

"There is no single best premium flagship, as consumer priorities vary. As Apple and Samsung flagship prices move towards ₹2 lakh, tech-focused brands like iQOO and Google are attracting consumers with specifications that are at par but at more competitive prices. Beyond hardware, ecosystem flexibility is becoming an important differentiator, especially for working professionals who tend to carry more than one smartphone in addition to a laptop," the report said.

Market leader Samsung recently increased the price of smartphones in the range of ₹2,000-₹4,000 apiece post Diwali.

Before Diwali, the firm had raised the price of its flagship device Galaxy S26 by 17 per cent.

Chinese smartphone company Xiaomi has also increased the price of devices in the same range after Diwali.
